newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian PM set to denounce Hanson on UK visit.
newsitem.headline: Australian PM set to denounce Hanson on UK visit.

text.p: Australian Prime Minister John Howard will use a high-profile speech in London next week to denounce populist politician Pauline Hanson as an extremist with little support in the Australian community.

Howard told a party room meeting of his Liberal-National coalition on Tuesday that Hanson was merely a product of economic and social change, similar to French far-right politician Jean-Marie Le Pen and U.S. former Ku Klux Klan leader David Duke, party spokesman Kevin Andrews told reporters.
"He said there's nothing unusual in Western societies which are undergoing enormous transition throwing up people with extreme views," Andrews said.

"He was talking about the fact that in a number of countries around the world there are people that have received attention whose views are not those necessarily embraced by the mainstream of those countries."
Andrews said Howard had cited Le Pen and Duke.
The conservative leader left Canberra on Tuesday for a 16-day visit to London, Washington and New York, dismissed by the Labor opposition as a mere summer jaunt.
Andrews said he expected Howard to denounce Hanson at a speech at London University on Monday.
Howard has been criticised for not quickly speaking out against Hanson after she sparked a divisive national race row last year with warnings that Australia was in danger of being swamped by Asians.
Hanson's policies -- which also reject Aboriginal welfare, immigration and foreign investment -- have struck a chord with many voters.
Deputy Prime Minister and National Party leader Tim Fischer has warned her controversial stand threatens Australia's lucrative trade with its booming Asian neighbours.
But opinion polls put support for her newly-formed One Nation Party at up to 10 percent, enough to make her the new third force in Australian politics.
Howard, Australia's chief monarchist and cricket fan, arrives in London on Wednesday on the first leg of his visit to Australia's two main Western allies since winning power 16 months ago.
But critics complain the main spin of his tour, at least on the London leg, is not politics, but cricket.
The right-arm off-spinner has at least three cricket-related appearances in London and may also take time off with wife Janette to attend the tennis at Wimbledon.
"Appearances at Lord's (cricket ground) and Wimbledon and the general jollies of what might have been acceptable in the 1950s is not what is acceptable now," Labor opposition leader Kim Beazley said.
Howard dismissed Beazley's attack as petty.
"That is the sort of mean, stupid, petty comment of an opposition that has no solution to today's problems," he told reporters at Canberra's military airport before leaving.
"It is important that governments of Australia know the personality of the new British government."
Howard arrives back in Australia on July 3.
